content.title: Thank you for your questions and feedback.
content.comment:
Thank you for the detailed review and thoughtful feedback. Below we address specific questions.

**Q: For temporal decomposition, running k parallel thread would require the solution of the first k timesteps, not the initial condition only. Traditional numeric methods only require the initial condition**

A: Thank you for your comments. This is true and we have added this limitation in section 5. However, we believe that it does not hurt the overall effectiveness of NeuralStagger as the cost of collecting the initial k-steps states by numerical solvers is neglectable for long time period simulation. In addition, in case we only need the solution in a coarse temporal resolution, the initial condition is enough.

**Q: The improvements in results are not that compelling, although they are superior in multiplicative scale. The authors may want to test on bigger grids than 64*64**

A: Thank you for your suggestion. As for larger-scale tests,  we have shown the results of the spatial decomposition in Section 4.2, where the grid is 100x300, which is 30 thousand grid points in total. Tackling large-scale PDE problems is non-trivial with current techniques and may require more effort including the neural network design. Considering that most recent papers with promising results are working on problems with 30 thousand grid points or below, e.g., neural stochastic PDE[1] and Clifford neural network[2], we think the current problem scale is sufficient for demonstrating its effectiveness.  We are working on further implementing the NeuralStagger to 3D problems and will present them in the future. 

**Q: In figure 5, put the ground truth as well for comparison**

A: Thank you for your suggestion. We have updated it in the revision. In figure 5, we added the ground truth for the Navier stokes equation with periodic boundary conditions and lid-driven cavity, while for the boundary conditions with obstacles, we add the benchmark result of UNet for comparison as the ground truth is not provided in the baseline paper.

**Q: An ablation study with the spatial decomposition removed would be a good idea for experiment here. In its current form, it is not clear as to where the current improvements are coming from mostly, whether from spatial or temporal.**

A: Thank you for your suggestion. We have added another experiment with only temporal decomposition in Table 1. We admit that the current metrics can not describe where the improvement comes from as the computing sources are too strong to show the difference of elapsed time between large and small models. We have added a more detailed comparison to show the improvements in efficiency via the GMACs per card. Then we could clearly know the contribution of spatial and temporal decomposition. 

[1] Salvi, C., Lemercier, M., & Gerasimovics, A. (2021). Neural Stochastic Partial Differential Equations: Resolution-Invariant Learning of Continuous Spatiotemporal Dynamics. *arXiv preprint arXiv:2110.10249.* 

[2] Brandstetter, J., Berg, R. V. D., Welling, M., & Gupta, J. K. (2022). Clifford neural layers for pde modeling. *arXiv preprint arXiv:2209.04934.*

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper introduces NeuralStagger, a method to divide the spatial and temporal resolution into staggered coarser grids, and use a neural model to evolve the coarse-grained grids (which also takes the relative location of the coarser grid as input). In inference, the different grids are combined together reconstruct the original resolution as needed. The paper demonstrates in experiments that it has improved speed while sacrificing some accuracy compared to the full-resolution model. And the paper also show improved convergence time for one optimal control experiment. The paper also shows some guideline for how to choose the hyperparameter to balance the tradeoff.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
The paper is well written. The method is simple, and can be applied to general grid-based simulations.

Weaknesses:
1. Experiment evaluation:
The experiment evaluation is a little weak. 
(1) It is not clear how scalable the method is to problems with enough difficulty
It is not clear what is the Reynolds number of the flow through the cylinder problem is, and whether the Reynolds number is high enough to have vortex shedding (which is more difficult than laminar flow).

(2) It is not clear how the method is able to generalize to larger-scale problems. The flow through the cylinder is a relatively easy task. It would be great to demonstrate it in a larger-scale (potentially 3D) task, where neuralStagger is incorporated with a neural-based surrogate model. This is not necessary, but if NeuralStagger can scale to larger problems, it would strengthen the paper a lot.

(3) Why is in 4.1, only use the FNO to test, while in 4.2, only use the LordNet to test NeuralStagger? At least in section 4.2, would be great to have NeuralStagger combined with all of them (FNO and UNet), to show the generality of the method.

2. One potential weakness of the method is it may not generalize to the test dataset with a different domain geometry. Since in the training time, the relative position of the staggered grid is passed in as input, it breaks translational symmetry, and the model may learn the knowledge of how the relative position affect the evolution in this specific geometry. If in the test time, the geometry is different, such knowledge may not hold. From the current paper, it seems that the test geometry is the same as training time. It would be great to perform experiments showing what would happen if test geometry is different. For example, if the width and height of test grid is much larger, or if the cylinder location is different. If it shows certain generalization it will be great. If not show generalization that is fine, but state it clearly as limitation of the method.

3. It would be nice to state clearly the limitation of the work, e.g. the method in its current form only works for grid-based field (not irregular mesh)

A: Thank you for your comment, we have added the experiment details in the Appendix, and the Reynolds number here is 517, which is large enough to generate the vortex street. The test of the optimal control of vortex shedding frequency, where the Re is 880, also enough to have vortex shedding, can also demonstrate the scalability of the method to the difficult problem. 

**Q: It is not clear how the method is able to generalize to larger-scale problems. The flow through the cylinder is a relatively easy task. It would be great to demonstrate it in a larger-scale (potentially 3D) task, where neuralStagger is incorporated with a neural-based surrogate model. This is not necessary, but if NeuralStagger can scale to larger problems, it would strengthen the paper a lot.**

A: Thank you for your suggestion. NeuralStagger is easy to implement for the arbitrary case with regular mesh. The cylinder problem resolves the vortex-shedding phenomenon. The mesh size is 100x300, with 30 thousand grid points in total. Tackling large-scale PDE problems is non-trivial with current techniques and may require more effort including the neural network design. Considering that most recent papers with excellent results are working on problems with 30 thousand grid points or below, e.g., neural stochastic PDE [2] and Clifford neural network [3], we think the current problem scale is sufficient for demonstrating its effectiveness.  As for the 3D task, it is always a good thing to do and we are running the experiment in 3D flow-around-obstacle settings and will present them in our future work and presentation.

**Q: Why is in 4.1, only use the FNO to test, while in 4.2, only use the LordNet to test NeuralStagger? At least in section 4.2, would be great to have NeuralStagger combined with all of them (FNO and UNet), to show the generality of the method.**

A: In section 4.1, we hope to focus on the performance of the neuralStagger, so we choose the well-known FNO as the benchmark to test. Thank you for your suggestion, we have added the test of FNO and Unet in the appendix. For UNet, NeuralStagger can accelerate it with little drop in accuracy. As under the vanilla physics constrained training, FNO performs relatively weak, the performance of its NeuralStagger version is also poor. 

**Q: One potential weakness of the method is it may not generalize to the test dataset with a different domain geometry. Since in the training time, the relative position of the staggered grid is passed in as input, it breaks translational symmetry, and the model may learn the knowledge of how the relative position affect the evolution in this specific geometry. If in the test time, the geometry is different, such knowledge may not hold. From the current paper, it seems that the test geometry is the same as training time. It would be great to perform experiments showing what would happen if test geometry is different. For example, if the width and height of test grid is much larger, or if the cylinder location is different. If it shows certain generalization it will be great. If not show generalization that is fine, but state it clearly as limitation of the method.**

A: Thank you for your suggestion. In Section 4.2, the geometry of the testing, e.g. the locations of the cylinder and the pipe are randomly selected which are different from the ones in the training and they perform well. However, generalizing to different shapes of grids, e.g., those with higher resolution, also requires NN to be capable of handling different shapes of input. This is an interesting direction for future work, but may not be the aim of this paper.

**Q: It would be nice to state clearly the limitation of the work, e.g. the method in its current form only works for the grid-based field (not irregular mesh)**

A: Thank you for your suggestion, we have added the discussion in section 5. Applying NeuralStagger to irregular mesh is an interesting direction for future work.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper aims to speed up neural PDE solvers. The strategy is to decompose the spatial and temporal domains into smaller problems and use multiple neural networks to learn solutions to smaller problems in parallel. The paper presented results on Navier-Stokes equations.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
My overall feeling is that the paper is inadvertently revisiting a number of existing ideas in numerical methods for solving PDEs, and this paper gets a bit too excited about the speed obtained from this decomposition strategy but does not fully reveal its shortcomings to the readers. The staggered grid in Fig. 1 is not novel: Using central difference schemes in finite different methods often leads to these subgrids independent of each other. While this paper argues having small, independent subgrids are good for parallelism, classic numerical methods are much more concerned with its disadvantages not mentioned in the paper, e.g., high-frequency (in the spatial domain) errors are difficult to kill in such schemes.

The spatial decomposition method seems tied to rectangular domains that can be perfectly discretized with lattice grids only. I don’t see an easy way to adapt this method to irregular boundaries or couple it with triangular/tetrahedral discretization. This should be made clear at the beginning or discussed in the limitation section.

The staggered time integration idea can also be seen from classic numerical time integration schemes like Leapfrog integration/Verlet integration, but I don’t see a strong motivation for marrying it with neural networks: isn’t it actually much more difficult to predict the state after sT time steps than predict what will happen in the next time step?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
I will list my questions as I go through the paper:

Related work: It looks like this section ignores classic numerical PDE solvers and claims “two mainstream approaches…for solving PDEs” are both neural network methods. It is probably a good idea to at least mention some numerical methods like finite differences/elements/volumes, method of lines, etc. In particular, two classic ideas that are highly relevant to what this paper proposes are domain decomposition and multigrid solvers, which I think are quite worth discussing.

Sec. 3.2: Fig. 1 shows the coarse-resolution fields from spatial decomposition overlap each other, but the main text around Eqn. (5) seems to imply that spatial decomposition partitions the whole field into non-overlapping areas. Could you clarify which is the correct description of your method? Does sH x sW = 2 x 2 or 4 x 4 in your Fig. 1? I assumed that Fig. 1 is the factual description of the method when reviewing this paper.

Sec. 3.3: At a high level, I feel that what this section attempts to develop is already covered in the standard CFL conditions of a numerical PDE method. It would be good if the section could make a connection to CFL conditions and comment on what is new here.

Experiments: It looks like the experiments aim to show the model can generalize to different initial conditions, but I couldn’t find detailed descriptions of this. I would like to see how the initial conditions are generated (probably sampled from a random distribution?), and how different are them in the training and test sets. Maybe I missed some text in the supplemental material?

A small thing: The notation “S(u, a)” is inconsistent with the definition “S: A x U”. Please swap either (u, a) or A x U.

content.title: Thank you for your questions and feedback
content.comment:
Thank you for your time. We would like to stress several key points which would lead you in the right direction (maybe figure 1 led to a misunderstanding and we have slightly modified it) about the contribution and novelty of our method. We would like to stress that the spatially decomposed subgrids are evenly spread over the whole domain. I understand this is what you mean “overlapping”. The index i, j' in equation 5 represents the relative position of each sub-grid and in the case in Fig 1, sH=sW=2 and `i,j' equals (0, 0), (1, 0), (0, 1) and (1, 1) respectively. In terms of the relationship between NeuralStagger and numerical techniques like staggered mesh and leapfrog method, we would like to stress that they just look alike on the surface but are quite different in essence. For example, both the classical leap-frog integration and staggered mesh place the meshes of two variables with an offset to get a better discretization approximation. In contrast, NeuralStagger decomposes the mesh of a single variable into several interleaving sub-meshes and set up the independent learning tasks for the neural network. NeuralStagger and those numerical techniques are orthogonal and typically in the flow-around-obstacle cases, we use staggered-grid to define the high-resolution physics-constrained loss. NeuralStagger targets the physics-constrained training to get a couple of coarse-resolution NN solvers that run in parallel to accelerate both the high and coarse-resolution simulations. This is the first paper on this topic as far as we know and it shows great potential for simulation and inverse problems. Below we address specific questions.

**Q: My overall feeling is that the paper is inadvertently revisiting a number of existing ideas in numerical methods for solving PDEs, and this paper gets a bit too excited about the speed obtained from this decomposition strategy but does not fully reveal its shortcomings to the readers. The staggered grid in Fig. 1 is not novel: Using central difference schemes in finite different methods often leads to these subgrids independent of each other. While this paper argues having small, independent subgrids are good for parallelism, classic numerical methods are much more concerned with its disadvantages not mentioned in the paper, e.g., high-frequency (in the spatial domain) errors are difficult to kill in such schemes.**

A: As we stated above, NeuralStagger is essentially different from those numerical methods. Those numerical methods are orthogonal to NeuralStagger and can be leveraged to define the high-resolution physics constrained loss. In other words, our method is general for other numerical schemes. Here we demonstrate the case which can be stably solved by finite difference. In the future, we will extend it to other schemes.

For our method, although the representation is for coarse-resolution solutions, the training loss is defined on the high-resolution solutions, which are produced by the multiple evaluations of the neural networks followed by merging based on the spatial points. Then the final neural networks output could satisfy the original physical rules and resolve the high frequency parts in the solution. As NeuralStagger handles the machine learning problem, we believe it is more related to discussing the information loss by the mesh decomposition and the difficulty of the learning task, which is already discussed in section 3.3.

**Q: The staggered time integration idea can also be seen from classic numerical time integration schemes like Leapfrog integration/Verlet integration, but I don’t see a strong motivation for marrying it with neural networks: isn’t it actually much more difficult to predict the state after sT time steps than predict what will happen in the next time step?**

A: As we stated previously, leap-frog and NeuralStagger are fundamentally different. Our motivation to predict after sT time steps is acceleration, e.g., fewer time steps for long time period simulation. But the leapfrog integration is to update the position and velocity at interleaved time points for better stability and accuracy. For high-resolution simulation, our neuralStagger in the temporal direction is a simple decomposition which means we learn the neural PDE solver (u_{t+k} = f(u_t)) with large time step with the physics-constrained loss, and then decompose the original u_{t:t+k-1} into k snapshots, evaluate with neural network f for every snapshot, finally, we get the u_{t+k:t+2*k-1} and the time step reduced to 1. Though learning to predict sT time steps ahead was done in several supervised learning tasks, it has not been realized in physics-constrained training, because the physics-constrained loss with a large time step is unstable. With the approach, we could easily roll out the simulation with neutral networks and also could produce high-resolution outputs simultaneously.

content.comment:
**Q: The spatial decomposition method seems tied to rectangular domains that can be perfectly discretized with lattice grids only. I don’t see an easy way to adapt this method to irregular boundaries or couple it with triangular/tetrahedral discretization. This should be made clear at the beginning or discussed in the limitation section.**

A: Thank you for your suggestion. We have added that in the revision. For irregular meshes, spatial decomposition resembles the vertex coloring problem, which is NP-complete for the exact solution. However, we are optimistic about tackling this problem as there are heuristic methods to handle the problem efficiently with the trade-off of violating the coloring constraints in small parts of the graph, which we believe does not influence the effectiveness of

**Q: Related work: It looks like this section ignores classic numerical PDE solvers and claims “two mainstream approaches…for solving PDEs” are both neural network methods. It is probably a good idea to at least mention some numerical methods like finite differences/elements/volumes, method of lines, etc. In particular, two classic ideas that are highly relevant to what this paper proposes are domain decomposition and multigrid solvers, which I think are quite worth discussing.**

A: Thank you for your suggestion, we have added them in the revision to help readers to avoid misunderstanding and be clear about the novelty of the approach.

**Q: Sec. 3.2: Fig. 1 shows the coarse-resolution fields from spatial decomposition overlap each other, but the main text around Eqn. (5) seems to imply that spatial decomposition partitions the whole field into non-overlapping areas. Could you clarify which is the correct description of your method? Does sH x sW = 2 x 2 or 4 x 4 in your Fig. 1? I assumed that Fig. 1 is the factual description of the method when reviewing this paper.**

A: Figure 1 is the factual description and we also slightly updated the Figure1 for better understanding. It is different from the staggered grid and domain decomposition in numerical methods.  For example, for a field u with a resolution of 64x64, the spatial decomposition with sH=sW=2 is done by splitting the original u[:64,:64] into sHxsW patches, which are u[0:64:2,0:64:2], u[1:64:2,0:64:2], u[0:64:2,1:64:2], u[1:64:2,1:64:2]. So the spatial domains after spatial decomposition are overlapped but for the subgrid, their grid points are different from each other.

**Q: Sec. 3.3: At a high level, I feel that what this section attempts to develop is already covered in the standard CFL conditions of a numerical PDE method. It would be good if the section could make a connection to CFL conditions and comment on what is new here.**

A: As is stated, our method is orthogonal to the numerical discretization techniques and can be applied to other numerical discretization techniques, as the discretization techniques define the loss, and our method assigns the coarse-grained input-output to sub-networks. CFL condition may guide us on setting $\Delta t$ for the physics-constrained loss, which is not the focus of this paper. In section 3.3, we mainly analyze the effect of decomposition factors by viewing NeuralStagger as a machine learning task, e.g., investigating the task difficulty and information loss of the input.

**Q: Experiments: It looks like the experiments aim to show the model can generalize to different initial conditions, but I couldn’t find detailed descriptions of this. I would like to see how the initial conditions are generated (probably sampled from a random distribution?), and how different are them in the training and test sets. Maybe I missed some text in the supplemental material?**

A: We add more details in the appendix. The initial conditions from sampled from a random distribution. We generate a lot of trajectories and use some of them for training and others for tests.

**Q: A small thing: The notation “S(u, a)” is inconsistent with the definition “S: A x U”. Please swap either (u, a) or A x U.**

A: Thanks for spotting the inconsistency. We have corrected this in the revision.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposes to address the challenge of learning models to predict the dynamics of fluid systems with high resolutions by interleaving discretization points spatially and temporally. I.e., under the assumption that solution is sufficiently continuous, multiple evaluations of a network can be used and evaluated in parallel. 

While the central goal of the paper is an important one, and the idea seems attractive at first, I'm less convinced after seeing the results: there seem to be clear limitations in terms of spatial "staggering", and the temporal one primarily means taking larger time steps. The latter also seems responsible for the majority of the speed up.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
In terms of positive aspects, the paper is clearly written, presents the results in a honest way. It also contains a good evaluation.

On the negative side, as mentioned above, I do have concerns over the general applicability of the decomposition. The main algorithmic change is due to the different spatial networks. Once the solutions become less smooth, I would expect these networks to have a harder time with accurately reproducing the solutions, as acknowledged in the text. The examples shown in the paper however focus on relatively small resolution changes, and smooth solutions.

The "temporal staggering" is fundamentally different in nature. This simply means training the network to directly produce solutions at a later time. It is not overly surprising (and was demonstrated in other papers) that a network can handle larger time steps and larger CFL conditions than regular solvers. It seems this is where most of the gains in performance come from.
 
Also, on the practical side it is not overly attractive having to deal with multiple piece-wise evaluations of the network (but this could of course potentially be hidden with suitable wrapper code).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is clearly written for the largest part, and the idea is original to the best of my knowledge. My main concerns are with the general usefulness of the proposed method.

Btw., I have a question for the authors here: how is the staggering related to the unsupervised training? Shouldn't it work similarly well if the data is precomputed using a supervised loss?

The related work is a bit strange, in my opinion. The CNN-based approach here seems to be more in line with works such as "Accelerating Eulerian Fluid Simulation With Convolutional Networks" from 2017 rather than with PINNs. And the "neural operator" label is typically reserved for continuous descriptions (along the lines of fourier features), rather than for "everything else than PINNs".
content.summary_of_the_review: It's definitely a good idea to aim for faster neural network based simulations. However, I don't find the approach taken here to be overly promising: leaving out samples in space and time is certainly possible for neural networks, and data-driven algorithms in general. I'm not convinced that this moves the paper above the ICLR threshold for acceptance.

content.title: Thank you for your questions and feedback
content.comment:
Thank you for the detailed review and thoughtful feedback. We would like to stress that our approach is fully unsupervised—NeuralStagger enables the physics constrained training for coarse-resolution neural PDE solvers, which was impossible in previous works as they must train the model with the resolution as high as numerical methods. Meanwhile, the NeuralStagger could make the inference of neural PDE solvers faster because it could parallel the inference both in spatial and temporal directions. Below we address specific questions.

**Q: The concerns over the general applicability of the decomposition.**.

A: Thank you for your comment. One purpose of this paper is to solve the problem of coarse-resolution simulation representation using physical loss. Although this is easily achieved with an NN trained with coarse-generated data via supervised training, training with physical loss is non-trivial because of the requirement of fine resolution (small time step and spatial interval) to achieve numerical stability and accuracy. Therefore, in order to accelerate the inference with a physical loss under the setting that data is not easy to obtain, we propose the NeuralStagger. The idea of the NeuralStagger is to split the original high-resolution neural PDE solver learning task into several subtasks of coarse-resolution neural PDE solver learning, then it could accelerate the inference of Neural PDE solver as the spatial and temporal inference could be both paralleled and also the physics-constrained learning for coarse-resolution fields has been solved under this framework. In theory, the grouped predictions of the subtasks can successfully reconstruct the non-smooth target solution (high-resolution) because the prediction of high resolution satisfies the PDE after the neural network is well-trained. But we recognize that less smooth solutions make generalization difficult and therefore require more data and a more powerful network, but supervised learning suffers from the same problem. So the limit of our decomposition is consistent with the coarse-grained spatial-temporal resolution that supervised learning can achieve, consistent with their applicability. This problem we believe will not be a critical problem when we feed the historical states as the supplement information to the NN solver, as mentioned in section5.

**Q: The "temporal staggering" is fundamentally different in nature. It is not overly surprising (and was demonstrated in other papers) that a network can handle larger time steps and larger CFL conditions than regular solvers. It seems this is where most of the gains in performance come from.**

A: Thank you. As we mentioned in your early question, one main difference is that we use Physics-constrained learning to achieve temporal decomposition. It is easy to achieve “temporal staggering” in supervised learning, but this is the first paper to achieve that in unsupervised (physics-based) learning way as far as we know. In terms of the source of performance gain, we would like to stress that the spatial gain is also significant. We apologize that the speed evaluation is misleading as it depends highly on GPU devices. When the GPU capability is sufficient even for the largest NN, e.g., A100 we use for speed test, the inference speed of NNs does not vary much. In the newest version of our paper, we also list the GMACs per inference of all NNs in table 1, which clearly shows that the load of each computational node drops fast with growing factors.

**Q: How is the staggering related to the unsupervised training? Shouldn't it work similarly well if the data is precomputed using a supervised loss?**

A: Thank you. The whole story is that supervised learning will require massive pre-generated data and the generalization is not quite well. Unsupervised learning (physics-constrained learning) would address these issues well. However, the speed-up effect is relatively limited as the physics constrained loss forces the model to work in the same resolution as the numerical solutions, which is often high to prevent accuracy and stability issues.

**Q: However, I don't find the approach taken here to be overly promising: leaving out samples in space and time is certainly possible for neural networks, and data-driven algorithms in general.**

A: While the main goal of the approach is for physics constrained learning, we define a coarse-resolution neural solver for each subtask, which requires fewer computational resources, and jointly train them with the vanilla physics constrained loss by simply arranging their outputs to reconstruct the original solution. The final output of the networks could be multi-resolution and with the same computational performance due to the perfect perfect parallelism between the subtasks. The proposed method introduces a way for physics-constrained learning on coarse-resolution model, meanwhile parallelling the inference in spatial and temporal directions. This is unique.

content.title: Reply to other specific questions
content.comment:
**Q: On the practical side it is not overly attractive having to deal with multiple piece-wise evaluations of the network (but this could of course potentially be hidden with suitable wrapper code)**.

A: For the case where we hope to roll out the physical process, or the application in inverse problems (shown in Section 4.3), the multiple piece-wise evaluations would introduce efficiency improvements a lot. It is relatively easy to implement a wrapper for general NNs by decomposing the input or reconstructing the output with tensor operations in modern deep learning frameworks, e.g., PixelShuffle in PyTorch.

**Q: The CNN-based approach here seems to be more in line with works such as "Accelerating Eulerian Fluid Simulation With Convolutional Networks" from 2017 rather than with PINNs.**

A: Thank you for your suggestion. We have added the citation and polished the related work section. You may kindly refer to the newest version.

content.title: Acknowledgement of the response
content.comment: Thank you for the clarifications and the various smaller updates to the paper. Taking into account the current state and comments by the other reviewers, I'm still learning towards the negative side (keeping my rating unchanged). I'd recommend to provide more insights and emphasis on the physics-based/unsupervised temporal staggering, and include experiments to clearly separate and show the gains for space and time.

display_title: Thank you all for your questions and feedback

content.title: Thank you all for your questions and feedback
content.comment:
We would like to thank reviewers for providing high-quality reviews and constructive feedback that have improved the paper. We are encouraged that reviewers think our paper is “well written, the method is novel and simple, can be applied to general grid-based simulation” (Reviewer frLw), “clearly written and the central goal of the paper is an important one” (Reviewer wnZL), “novel and the authors tackle an important problem of solving PDEs in an efficient manner” (Reviewer Lisi).

We have updated our draft to further improve the writing and incorporate suggestions (marked in the revision) from reviewers and extended the appendix with more details about experiments. Below, we list the details and reply to the questions.
